instructions:
Read the paper below and produce a structured summary.

It matched these tracked topics; `relevance` must contain one entry per slug, stating what this paper changes for that topic:
- overthinking: Overthinking — When and why large reasoning models think more than a problem needs (or less than it needs) — the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff of reasoning length, test-time compute scaling, and methods to make a model stop, or keep going, at the right point.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what

payload.title: Evaluating Judges as Evaluators: The JETTS Benchmark of LLM-as-Judges as Test-Time Scaling Evaluators

contributions: Introduces the JETTS benchmark spanning three domains (math, code, instruction-following) and three test-time-scaling settings (response reranking, step-level beam search, critique-based refinement)
Compares ten judge models (7B-70B) against eight base generator models and against outcome/process reward models
Finds that judges match outcome reward models in response selection but underperform process reward models in beam search
Finds that judges' natural-language critiques are currently ineffective at guiding a generator toward better responses
result.method: Evaluates ten LLM judge models, ranging from 7B to 70B parameters, as evaluators guiding three test-time-scaling protocols -- response reranking, step-level beam search, and critique-based response refinement -- against eight base generator models, and compares judge performance to dedicated outcome and process reward models.
result.one_liner: JETTS is a benchmark evaluating how well LLM-as-judge models perform as evaluators guiding test-time-scaling methods -- response reranking, step-level beam search, and critique-based refinement -- across math, code and instruction-following.
result.problem: Scaling test-time computation typically relies on external non-generative evaluators (verifiers, reward models) to select or guide extra compute, but how well general-purpose LLM judges perform this evaluator role, compared to purpose-built reward models, had not been systematically tested.

relevance.overthinking: Evaluates the judges/verifiers that decide how test-time compute is allocated across candidates (reranking, beam search, refinement), rather than reasoning length itself. It is a real, direct contribution to the test-time-compute-scaling side of this topic -- showing judges are competitive at selection but weak at beam search and at critique-guided refinement -- though its focus is evaluator quality rather than the stop/continue decision within a single chain of thought.

result.results: Judges matched outcome reward models in response reranking/selection but underperformed process reward models in step-level beam search; judges' natural-language critiques were found ineffective at guiding the generator toward better responses.
